passage:
Tuesday
The coaching institute's ad was everywhere today: "95% of our students placed!" and a wall of smiling faces. Lokesh has already paid the deposit. I almost did too.
But at the counselling desk I asked: 95% of whom? Turns out it's 95% of students who finished and sat the final test. How many joined? The man at the desk got vague. Lokesh's senior told us half the batch dropped out by month three. So maybe it's more like half of half.
Not saying it's bad. Maybe it's great. But before I pay anything, I'm going to find five people who joined and didn't finish, and ask them what happened.
Shankar

qa.q: What did the coaching institute's ad say?
qa.a: 95% of our students placed, with a wall of smiling faces.

qa.q: Why did Shankar ask '95% of whom?'
qa.a: Shankar felt doubtful that the smiling faces showed everyone, suspecting they were only those who finished, and wanted to know about everyone who joined.

qa.q: What makes Shankar's plan a sensible one?
qa.a: Talking to five people who joined and didn't finish shows the whole group, including the missing ones, before any money is paid.

qa.q: How might Lokesh feel after hearing Shankar's questions?
qa.a: Lokesh, who already paid the deposit, might feel uneasy or defensive, but also prompted to ask what happened to the dropouts.

grounding: Someone in their mid-twenties asks what the full batch looked like, including dropouts, before trusting a course's success figure.

Arohi: hmm. how many reps do it in total?
Kamal: no idea. why

Kamal: but the top 3 swear by it
Arohi: sure. i'd just like to see the whole team. who does it, who doesn't, and how they're all doing
Kamal: you want a spreadsheet for waking up 😅

Arohi: thanks. if it holds up, i'll set my alarm too 🙂

qa.q: Who does the boss say all do the 5 am routine?
qa.a: The top 3 sales reps all do it.

qa.q: What is Arohi worried the boss is missing?
qa.a: Arohi worries the boss sees only the top 3, not the other people who follow the routine and aren't doing great.

qa.q: Why is Arohi's request for the whole team's numbers useful?
qa.a: Comparing everyone who does and doesn't follow the routine shows whether it really helps, before 40 people change their sleep.

qa.q: How does Kamal first see Arohi's question?
qa.a: Kamal finds it a bit funny, joking about a spreadsheet for waking up, but agrees to ask Meena for the numbers.

grounding: A professional asks how the whole team is doing before praising a routine copied from the top sellers.

passage: At the panchayat meeting in Dhanauri, a seed dealer pointed to three farmers in the front row. "All three used our new wheat seed, and all three doubled their harvest!" Heads nodded. Shreya, the young agriculture extension worker, raised her hand. "How many farmers in the block bought this seed last season?" The dealer hesitated. "Around forty." "And the other thirty-seven?" Nazia, a farmer at the back, called out, "My field had the same seed. Half of it failed." Two more hands went up. Shreya kept her voice friendly. "Maybe it's a good seed. But before the panchayat praises it, let's hear from all forty, and check whose fields had canal water." The dealer's smile tightened. The three in the front row shifted in their seats.

qa.q: How many farmers bought the new seed last season, according to the dealer?
qa.a: Around forty.

qa.q: Why did Shreya ask about the other thirty-seven?
qa.a: Shreya felt doubtful that the three in the front row told the whole story, and wanted to see the whole group before praising the seed.

qa.q: What does Shreya propose the panchayat do next?
qa.a: Hear from all forty farmers and check whose fields had canal water before praising the seed.

qa.q: How might Nazia feel when Shreya's question gives her a chance to speak?
qa.a: Nazia, whose field half failed, may feel relieved that her loss finally counts in the story.

grounding: A young extension worker asks about all the farmers who used a seed, not just the three winners, before it is praised.

passage:
At the Copenhagen running club's Tuesday meeting, the coach pinned up photos of five members who'd run marathons under three hours. "All five used my twelve-week plan," she said. "It works."
Everyone clapped. Anders, twenty-five, raised a hand. "How many people started the plan?"
The coach blinked. "Around forty last year."
"And the other thirty-five?"
There was a pause. Emil, beside him, whispered, "Mate, don't ruin it."
"I'm not," Anders said quietly. "I want to join. I just want to know what happened to everyone else."
The coach checked her notes. Twelve had dropped out injured. Eight had finished slower than before. The rest had improved a little.
"So it helps some people," Anders said, "and hurts some. That's useful to know." He signed up, but asked for the injury-prevention sessions too.

qa.q: How many people started the plan last year, according to the coach?
qa.a: Around forty last year.

qa.q: What did Anders want when he asked about the other thirty-five?
qa.a: He wanted to know what happened to everyone who tried the plan, not only the five winners, because he was genuinely interested in joining and wanted the full picture.

qa.q: How did asking about the missing runners change Anders's choice?
qa.a: Learning that twelve had dropped out injured led him to sign up but also ask for the injury-prevention sessions.

qa.q: How might Emil see Anders's question at first?
qa.a: Emil seems embarrassed at first, thinking Anders is spoiling the celebration, not seeing that the question helps everyone decide sensibly.

grounding: It shows a thoughtful person asking about all who tried a training method, including those who failed, before praising it.

passage:
At the staff meeting of the Pune secondary school, the principal held up three board exam toppers' photos. "All three attended Mr. Gokhale's weekend crash course. I'm proposing every Class 10 student joins next year."
Heads nodded. Irawati, a second-year maths teacher, looked at the photos, then raised her hand. "How many students attended in total?"
Asif, the admissions clerk, checked. "Sixty-two."
"And how did the other fifty-nine do?"
The room went quiet. Asif pulled up the marks. Some had improved, some had dropped, and many were unchanged. Two parents had complained their children were exhausted.
"Maybe it helps some students," Irawati said. "I'd like to know which ones before we make it compulsory. And the three toppers were already scoring high in Class 9."
The principal frowned, then nodded. "Asif, get me the full list, before and after."

qa.q: How many students attended the crash course in total?
qa.a: Sixty-two.

qa.q: Why did Irawati raise her hand after seeing the photos?
qa.a: She felt that three toppers alone didn't show whether the course worked, and wanted to see the whole group before praising it.

qa.q: What did Irawati's questions lead the principal to decide?
qa.a: The principal asked Asif for the full list of marks before and after, instead of making the course compulsory straight away.

qa.q: How might the parents who complained feel if the course became compulsory?
qa.a: They would probably feel ignored, since their children found it exhausting and their experience would have been hidden behind the three toppers' photos.

grounding: It shows a teacher asking what happened to all the students who took a course, not only the toppers, before praising it.
